excerpt.en: Critical thinking usually points outward. But the hardest and most useful place to aim it is at the half-formed idea you almost dismissed as yours.
excerpt.de: Kritisches Denken richtet sich meist nach außen. Doch der schwierigste und nützlichste Ort dafür ist die halbfertige Idee, die du fast als deine eigene abgetan hättest.

body.en:
We're trained to aim critical thinking outward — at claims, sources, other people's arguments. The move I had to learn was aiming it inward, at my own half-formed thoughts, *before* dismissing them.

Most ideas die young. Not because they're wrong, but because we don't extend them the courtesy of being evaluated at all. The thought shows up, feels unserious, and gets waved off.

## Taking a thought seriously means

- Writing it down before judging it.
- Asking "what would have to be true for this to be right?" instead of "is this dumb?"
- Giving it the same charitable reading I'd give a stranger's argument.

## The failure mode on both sides

- Too little seriousness: every original thought gets pre-emptively deleted.
- Too much: every passing notion becomes a conviction. Seriousness is *evaluation*, not adoption.

## Why it matters more now

When answers are cheap and everywhere, the scarce thing is a point of view. That only develops if you treat your own raw material as worth refining.

## Notes to self

- Distinguish "take seriously" from "believe." The whole essay hinges on that line.
- Personal example of a thought I almost threw away.
